title: Mine, yours
goal: Use the three sets of personal pronouns, express ownership with *ko/mo/niya*, and answer the question *kanino*.
bekal: say whose something is with two patterns: *bahay ko* and *akin ang bahay*
tell *tayo* (we, including you) from *kami* (we, excluding you) — a distinction English doesn't make
put *ka*, *ko* and *mo* in the right place in a sentence

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Kaninong cellphone?
dialogs.intro: After class, a phone has been left on a table. Mia, Ana and Budi try to find its owner.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.id: I don't know. It's not mine.

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Hindi. Ang cellphone ko ay nasa bag ko.
lines.id: No. My phone is in my bag.
lines.literal: no. si phone my is located-in bag my.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Baka kay Kuya Ben. Siya ang huling umalis.
lines.id: Maybe it's Kuya Ben's. He was the last one to leave.
lines.literal: maybe to-si Kuya Ben. he si last who-left.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Tama ka. Kanila ang mga gamit sa mesa.
lines.id: You're right. The things on the table are theirs.
lines.literal: right you. theirs si plural things on table.

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Sige, ibalik natin sa kaniya bukas.
lines.id: Okay, let's give it back to him tomorrow.
lines.literal: all-right, return our to him tomorrow.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Natin? Kami ni Ana ang uuwi ngayon, hindi ikaw!
lines.id: Let's? Ana and I are the ones going home today, not you!
lines.literal: our-incl? we with-si Ana si the-ones-going-home today, not you!

lines.speaker: Mia:
lines.text: Sorry! Ibalik ninyo pala, hindi natin.
lines.id: Sorry! You two should return it, not us.
lines.literal: sorry! return your-plural it-turns-out, not our-incl.

lines.speaker: Ana:
lines.text: Ayan, tama na ang Tagalog mo!
lines.id: There you go, your Tagalog is already correct!
lines.literal: there, right now si Tagalog your!

notes: **Ownership has two patterns.** The first attaches a short pronoun behind the thing: *bahay ko* (my house), *cellphone mo* (your phone). The second puts a long form in front: *akin ang bahay* (the house is mine). The first is for naming, the second for stating who owns it.
**Kanino means "whose".** With the linker it becomes *kaninong*: *Kaninong cellphone ito?* The answer uses the *sa* forms: *akin*, *iyo*, *kaniya*, or *kay* + name: *kay Ben*.

**Tayo and kami both mean "we", but they're not the same.** *Tayo* includes the person you're talking to — "you and I and maybe others". *Kami* excludes them: "we, but not you". English has no such split, so think of *tayo* as "we (including you)" and *kami* as "we (not you)". Fun fact: Malay and Indonesian make the same distinction (*kita* / *kami*), so this is a well-known Austronesian feature.

**Ang cellphone ko ay nasa bag ko** uses *ay*, which makes the sentence sound tidy and a bit formal. In ordinary conversation: *Nasa bag ko ang cellphone ko.* The place first, the spotlighted thing last.

**Baka means "maybe"** and is read *bah-KAH'* with stress at the end. With stress at the front (*BAH-kah*), it means "cow". One of the stress pairs Filipinos most often joke about with foreign learners.

**Kami ni Ana** literally means "we with Ana" and means "Ana and I". This is a typical Tagalog pattern: plural pronoun + *ni* + name. Compare *tayo ni Ana* (you, me and Ana), *sila ni Ben* (he/she and Ben).
**Pala marks surprise** — "oh, so it turns out". It's one of the most useful and distinctive particles; its full chapter is in unit 14. For now just feel its tone: *Ikaw pala!* = "oh, it's you!"
**Ayan** (from *iyan*) is used like "there you go" in English — to mark that something has finally worked out.
**Tama na** literally means "right now" and means "enough" or "that's just right". Very often used to stop something politely: *Tama na po* — "that's enough, thank you".

grammars.title: Three sets of personal pronouns
body: Tagalog uses three forms for each person, and all three must be learned together, not one by one. The sets are named after the marker they replace: the *ang* set, the *ng* set and the *sa* set.
after: **Ikaw stands in front, ka attaches behind.** *Ikaw ang guro* (you're the teacher) but *Guro ka* (you're a teacher). The rule is simple: if the word starts the sentence, use *ikaw*; if not, use *ka*.
The *sa* set is also used after prepositions: *sa akin* (to me), *para sa iyo* (for you), *kasama nila* (with them).
The polite form to one person uses the plural forms: *kayo*, *ninyo*, *inyo* — just like *vous* in French or *usted*-style formality in many languages.

grammars.title: Two ways to say ownership
body: The difference between them isn't right versus wrong, but what you're putting in the spotlight.
after: For people's names, the *ng* set becomes **ni** and the *sa* set becomes **kay**: *libro ni Ben*, *kay Ben ang libro*. The plural forms are *nina* and *kina*.
There's a third, longer form: *ang bahay na akin* or *ang aking bahay*. The last one is often used in writing and speeches, and its order is the reverse of the usual: *ang aking pangalan* = my name.
⚠️ Don't mix the two patterns: *akin ang bahay ko* means "my house is mine" — grammatical but going in circles.

blocks.text: *Ka*, *ko*, *mo* and their friends are words that can't stand alone: they must lean on another word. Their place is always **after the first word** of the sentence.

Notice *hindi ko alam* — not *hindi alam ko*. Because *hindi* is the first word, all the short words gather right after it. You'll say this sentence dozens of times a day as a beginner, so memorize the whole form.

blocks.title: Two short words at once
items: If there are two, the one that goes first is the **one-syllable** one: *Ibigay mo sa akin* but *Ibigay mo ito sa akin*.
The combination *ko* + *ikaw* has a special form you must memorize: **kita**. *Mahal kita* = "I love you", not *mahal ko ikaw*. This form exists only for the pair I→you.

blocks.text: Notice how many English words are used as they are. For modern objects, Filipinos almost always use the English word — forcing a Tagalog equivalent for *cellphone* or *laptop* just makes you sound like an old textbook.
